transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-08-18
- Time: 14:00 PDT
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Elena Voss (CTO - BatchCraft), Marcus Li (SRE), Priya Nair (ML Eng)

Summary: quick retune standup to look at last 48h steady-state run, address p95 spikes when traffic bursts, and confirm next-step artifacts.

Transcript:
[00:00:01] Jordan: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick agenda — recap the last run, dig into the spike window, propose retune steps, agree artifacts. does that work?
[00:00:12] Elena: yes, that sounds good. we've got Marcus and Priya on for the logs.
[00:00:18] Marcus: hi all.
[00:00:20] Priya: hey.
[00:00:22] Samir: hey team, i'll share my screen in a sec with the batch histograms and queue depth timeline. just a heads up — we pulled the run where you flipped continuous batching on at 03:00 and then enabled a higher concurrency cap at 04:00, so we can see both transitions.
[00:00:35] Jordan: perfect. quick clarification — when you say higher concurrency cap, that's the client-side concurrency target, right? not the Redwood routing cap?
[00:00:42] Priya: it's both, actually. our workload orchestration bumped client concurrency from 8 to 20 during a traffic surge pattern. we left the platform default at 16 but there was a transient mismatch.
[00:00:52] Samir: yeah and that mismatch is key. what we saw was the client opened more inflight requests than the runtime could aggregate into efficient batches, so you get smaller batch sizes and more scheduling overhead, which pushes p95 up.
[00:01:05] Elena: hm, ok so it's like squandered batching efficiency. is that something we can fix purely on Redwood side?
[00:01:11] Samir: partly. we can tune the batching window and priority for prefix cache matches; we can also apply soft backpressure — slow the acceptance rate from the router for this customer route to let batches form. but if the client keeps firing concurrently it still increases queue depth.
[00:01:26] Marcus: i noticed that during the spike our KV cache hit rate dropped by about 12%. the traces show a lot of short-lived conversation IDs — likely due to our frontend spawning fresh sessions.
[00:01:36] Priya: yeah we traced that to a retry loop in our edge lambda — it's creating new conversation IDs on 429s.
[00:01:41] Jordan: okay so two levers — client behavior (fix retries, reuse conv IDs) and runtime tunables (batch window, concurrency caps, fallback). which do we want to prioritize?
[00:01:50] Elena: I'd rather fix client retry logic but that may take a sprint; in the meantime we need robust fallback so customer-facing SLAs don't degrade.
[00:01:58] Samir: agreed. operationally we recommend three things: 1) adjust continuous batching target to prefer slightly larger batch sizes under this workload (increase batching max_wait from 8ms to 15ms), 2) enable route-level soft backpressure with a queue threshold at 120 requests, and 3) configure burst capacity fallback to a slightly higher model variant when latency crosses 700ms for p95.
[00:02:19] Marcus: can you explain the model variant fallback — won't switching models change token quality?
[00:02:24] Samir: yes it can. the fallback would be to a quantized variant that's faster but slightly lower sampling entropy. we set it as a last-resort option so that user-facing latency stays within SLO while we heal the root cause.
[00:02:36] Priya: what's the expected unit cost delta if we enable permanent burst capacity?
[00:02:40] Jordan: i'll send numbers after the call but rough ballpark is +18–28% during sustained bursts; the billing is measured on reserved pool utilization plus burst time.
[00:02:48] Priya: okay.
[00:02:50] [00:03:01] Samir: i'm switching to the histogram — you can see batch size distribution pre/post retune. between 03:00–03:30, batch median dropped from 12 to 5 then recovered. the p95 latency tracks inversely.
[00:03:15] Marcus: that matches our downstream queue build-up logs. there were spikes around 03:14 and 03:22 with a downstream retry cascade.
[00:03:23] Jordan: are we seeing any evidence that the runtime is dropping KV cache entries too aggressively?
[00:03:28] Samir: yes a little — eviction rate ticked up during the high concurrency window because the KV footprint is proportional to active conversations. we can change the eviction policy to favor prefix retention for the first 60s of a conversation which increases hit rate.
[00:03:42] Priya: that seems useful. any memory cost?
[00:03:45] Samir: modest — about 6–8% increase in working set for your current model, but it recovers after idle windows.
[00:03:52] Elena: we can accept some memory increase if p95 is stable.
[00:03:55] [00:04:10] Jordan: okay let's map this into concrete steps. Samir — you'll run a 6-hour steady-state with these changes: batching max_wait 15ms, KV prefix retention 60s, soft backpressure threshold 120. capture batch distribution and p50/p95. Marcus/Priya — export the 24h trace and also sanitize the conversation IDs.
[00:04:28] Marcus: yes we'll get the trace out.
[00:04:30] Priya: quick Q — for soft backpressure, do you have an SDK knob or is it config on the Redwood console?
[00:04:36] Samir: it's a route-level policy on the console plus an optional header you can set from the client for preferred concurrency. we can push a recommended config snippet.
[00:04:45] Jordan: i'll add that snippet to the follow-up.
[00:04:48] [00:05:00] Elena: another question — audit/compliance: do these retunes change any data residency or logging? our security team will ask.
[00:05:07] Samir: they don't change data residency. we will increase a small set of routing telemetry and batch metrics but everything is logged per your SOC 2 controls, and we can limit retention if needed.
[00:05:16] Marcus: can you include the exact telemetry names? our SecOps wants precise fields for the audit doc.
[00:05:20] Samir: yep — i'll include the metric names and the schema in the follow-up.
[00:05:26] [00:05:36] Priya: oh and about the retry loop — we'll prototype a sticky conversation ID at the edge so retries reuse the same ID rather than spawn new ones. that's probably the biggest wins for KV hit rate.
[00:05:44] Samir: excellent. if you can flip that in a canary we can re-run the stress and measure delta.
[00:05:50] Jordan: timeline check — can we aim to have the artifacts in a week and the stress run by next Tuesday?
[00:05:56] Elena: yes that's fine.
[00:05:58] [00:06:10] Samir: one more nuance — under continuous batching there's sometimes a tradeoff where smaller user requests get held longer to make a batch which slightly affects tail latency for single-turn prompts. for your interactive flows we recommend an opt-out header for low-latency single-turn traffic.
[00:06:26] Marcus: can we map routes so that conversational flows benefit from batching but search-like single-shot queries bypass and get low-latency priming?
[00:06:33] Samir: absolutely, route tagging is supported. we'll add routing examples.
[00:06:40] [00:07:00] Jordan: let's capture risks — switching fallback model may change text variance, client retry fix takes engineering cycles, and permanent higher memory for KV retention. any other risks?
[00:07:10] Priya: potential cost increase if burst capacity is used frequently.
[00:07:13] Elena: and also we'd like to avoid quality regressions during A/B tests.
[00:07:18] Samir: we can gate fallback behind a canary and expose quality metrics during the canary run.
[00:07:24] [00:07:35] Jordan: ok final recap — action items as discussed. i'll send the pricing and playbook by tomorrow EOD. Samir will run the stress run and share logs. BatchCraft will provide traces and attempt the retry fix in canary. we reconvene same time next week unless something urgent pops up.
[00:07:52] Elena: thank you everyone.
[00:07:54] Marcus: thanks.
[00:07:55] Priya: thanks all.
[00:07:58] [00:58:00] Meeting ended.
